To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• We propose a novel reinforcement learning algorithm called posterior sampling for reinforcement (PSRL).
• PSRL achieves optimal regret bounds in the finite-horizon setting, and • PSRL achieves nearly optimal regret bounds in infinite-horizon discounted settings.
• We introduce posterior sampling for reinforcement-learning (PSRL), which samples policies from a posterior distribution over policies.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: Can we design efficient reinforcement learning algorithms? In particular, our work has been concerned with designing algorithms that are provably efficient, and that are simple to implement in practice.
developing algorithms that can solve the reinforcement learning problem efficiently.
developing new algorithms and theoretical analysis for reinforcement learning problems with large and/or continuous state-action spaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PSRL is an alternative to optimistic algorithms, with advantages for some problems, but worse performance for others.
“PSRL achieves a regret bound that is asymptotically optimal, but with a larger constant factor than that of UCRL2.

PSRL is the first algorithm for reinforcement learning with provably sublinear regret, and it is also the first provably efficient algorithm for reinforcement learning that does not introduce optimism in poorly understood states and/or actions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide the first regret bounds that hold for any unknown transition function.
we have developed a novel algorithm, posterior sampling for reinforcement Learning (PSRL), which achieves a regret bound of O(T3/4) in episodic MDP.
 We provide the first regret analysis for PSRL. 
The main takeaway from our work is that
posterior sampling is a powerful approach for efficient exploration in reinforcement reinforcement learning.
PSRL can be provably efficient, even when the underlying MDP is large and unknown.
posterior sampling for reinforcement learns as well as the best known algorithms for episodic reinforcement learning.
